Total_Summary_Deaths.Total_Deaths_Annotation: In all, the hurricane caused at least 164 deaths and $338,000 (1846 USD) in damage throughout its path,[nb 4] although some reports indicated hundreds of additional deaths across the island of Cuba.[1]

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: In Cuba, the hurricane's impact was extremely severe: the storm destroyed nearly a hundred ships and likely killed hundreds of individuals across the island,[1] while reports indicated the deaths of several dozen individuals during the entire course of the storm,[4] and other records noted that hundreds of deaths had possibly occurred across the island.[1]
In the United States, approximately $200,000 in damage and 40 deaths were reported,[9] representing four percent of the town's population.[18]

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Num: Teatro Principal obliterated; city gas plant unusable; numerous churches flattened; Havana Cathedral roof damaged; Montserrat Church unroofed; parish churches at Jesus del Monte destroyed; several hospitals including Real Hospital de San Lázaro demolished
Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: Masonry buildings bore the brunt of the storm, with the recently overhauled Teatro Principal wholly obliterated, the city gas plant rendered unusable, and numerous churches flattened. Havana Cathedral experienced damage to its roof, while the Montserrat Church was completely unroofed. The hurricane also destroyed parish churches at Jesus del Monte and Guanabacoa, while several hospitals, including the Real Hospital de San Lázaro, were demolished.

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: Not a single wharf at Baltimore, Maryland escaped the hurricane's storm surge, which inundated the length of Pratt Street along the shore; meanwhile, the Potomac River at Washington, D.C., and Alexandria, Virginia, attained its highest level in 20 years,[11]

To the north at Philadelphia, the tempest was the most intense in 30 years, with its high tides engulfing every wharf in the city; a total of 1.25 in (3.2 cm) of rain was measured at Pennsylvania Hospital. Despite widespread destruction along the Delaware River, damage to buildings in Philadelphia proper was less severe.[11]

In neighboring New Jersey, considerable damage to structures, timber, land, and livestock was observed, with winds toppling several buildings and trees; widespread rainfall, meanwhile, flooded salt marshes, also drowning cattle and sheep.[11]

Damage was similarly severe in New England, despite the storm's transition into a weaker extratropical cyclone. Significant damage was observed, with the waters of Upper New York Bay crashing over the Battery Park sea wall, washing away 300 ft (91 m) of its length.[12] Gusts caved in chimneys, uprooted trees, and sank several canal boats at the city's wharves.[20]

In the Boston area, a newly built brick residence's walls in the southern end of the city collapsed; on the other side of the city, a sawing and planing mill was razed to the ground.[20] Within the proximity of Boston at the towns of Canton and Southborough, winds obliterated two factories. High winds at Grafton collapsed the railroad sheds under the ownership of the Providence and Worcester Railroad. Malden endured the loss of a mansion which was still under construction, and several smaller buildings were also blown down there and at Monson. Winds upturned trees and toppled fences at Northampton, and nearby at Palmer, a school building was crumbled into pieces by intense winds. At Springfield, winds unroofed a repair facility at a local railroad depot and a house at the town armory. Gusts destroyed railroad sheds and factories in Stoughton and Worcester as well, and at Wilmington, winds crumbled a house into pieces.[20]

Time_Annotation: The origins of Tropical Storm Irma were from a subtropical depression that formed about 500 mi (800 km) south of the Azores on October 2. Time_Annotation: Around midday on October 8, the tropical depression strengthened into Tropical Storm Juliet; later, on October 11, Juliet merged with a frontal zone.

Hazards_Annotation: The storm’s maximum sustained winds of 50 mph indicate a wind hazard, and the reports of light rainfall (peaking at 4.51 in over Puerto Rico and up to 3 in over Bermuda) indicate a flood hazard.

Time_Annotation: On Saturday, November 11, 1911, a cold snap, known as the Great Blue Norther of 11/11/11, affected the Central United States. Some cities experienced tornadoes on Saturday and a blizzard on Sunday.

Hazards_Annotation: The article cites that some cities experienced tornadoes (a wind hazard) on Saturday, a blizzard on Sunday, and that the windy conditions upon front passage caused a dust storm in Oklahoma.

Time_Annotation: Dramatic cold snaps tend to occur mostly in the month of November, though they can also come in February or March.[5] Although temperature drops of this extent have happened on other occasions, as recently as February 2009, the fact that the 1911 cold front passage was during the autumn contributed to the properties mentioned in this article.[7]

Main_Event_Annotation: The text refers to a dramatic cold snap and significant temperature drops, indicating an extreme temperature event.

Time_Annotation: A westward-moving tropical wave from Africa entered the eastern Pacific in late August, organizing into a tropical depression at 12:00 UTC on August 30 south of the coastline of Mexico. The depression intensified into Tropical Storm Howard twelve hours later and further developed into a hurricane at 06:00 UTC on September 1. Howard degenerated into a remnant low at 18:00 UTC on September 5. The low turned southwest before dissipating over open waters on September 10.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Although the storm remained offshore, the outer bands produced significant flooding across the Baja California peninsula (in Mexico), with swells impacting the Baja California coastline as well as the California coastline in the United States, and moisture enhancing rainfall in parts of Arizona (United States).
Main_Event_Annotation: The system intensified into Tropical Storm Howard and then developed into a hurricane, ultimately reaching Category 4 status, which places it within the Tropical Storm/Cyclone category as defined by the Main_Event–Hazard association table.
Hazards_Annotation: At its peak, Hurricane Howard produced winds of 140 mph (indicating a wind hazard) and its outer bands caused significant flooding across the Baja California peninsula, damaging agricultural land and homes.

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: As it crossed Manitoulin Island just southeast of Sault Ste. Marie in Lake Huron, numerous trees were uprooted and some homes sustained heavy damage.

At about 17:30 EDT (21:30 UTC), the storm gathered further intensity before striking North Bay and the surrounding Nipissing District, where numerous trees were uprooted or snapped off and many buildings sustained heavy surface and some structural damage. Just south of the city, radio towers and a lighthouse were demolished by the violent winds.

Total_Summary_Affected.Total_Affected_Annotation: Through the next two hours the storm entered the Upper Ottawa Valley affecting places in Renfrew County such as Barry's Bay, Deep River, Cobden, Petawawa and Pembroke. Still, the storm carried a lot of lightning and damaging wind as it crossed portions of the Outaouais region – with impacts noted in Gatineau, extreme northern Ottawa, and areas including Chelsea, Cantley, La Peche, Notre-Dame-du-Laus and Kazabazua; additionally, the cities of Ottawa and Gatineau were brushed by the storm but escaped the worst of the effects.

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: Through the next two hours the storm entered the Upper Ottawa Valley affecting places in Renfrew County such as Barry's Bay, Deep River, Cobden, Petawawa and Pembroke.

The storm carried a lot of lightning and damaging wind as it crossed portions of the Outaouais region, the city of Gatineau and extreme northern portions of Ottawa at around 21:00 EDT. Areas such as Chelsea, Cantley, La Peche, Notre-Dame-du-Laus and Kazabazua were hit hard. The cities of Ottawa and Gatineau were brushed by the storm but escaped the worst of the effects.

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: In the Upper Gatineau north of the National Capital Region, several houses and cottages were damaged and scores of trees were snapped by winds in excess of 90 km/h (55 mph).
Meanwhile, in the Maniwaki area, a local radio station antenna suffered extensive damage.
Northwest of that town in Grand-Remous, several trailers in a park were heavily damaged or destroyed by the force of the winds.
Additional damage was reported in the Papineau region further east as well as in Mont-Laurier and the popular tourist village of Mont-Tremblant in the Upper Laurentians.

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: In mid-December, a significant Category 2 nor'easter affected much of the Northeastern United States with heavy snow and ice. Over 3 ft (0.91 m) of snow was reported across a swath in the interior Northeast, and the system caused seven fatalities.
In early February, a major Category 3 nor'easter, which started out as a winter storm on the West Coast, impacted an even larger area with heavy snow, also causing seven fatalities.

In mid-February, a series of two major Category 3 winter storms brought a swath of widespread snow and ice from the Pacific Northwest, through the Deep South, and to the Northeast. In total, the two winter storms resulted in at least $27.1 billion in damage, nearly 14 million power outages, and a total of 319 fatalities.

Event_Names: Deep Depression in the Bay of Bengal
Time_Annotation: A low-pressure area formed in the western Bay of Bengal on October 25. The IMD classified it as a depression on October 26, and later that day upgraded it to a deep depression. Moving northwestward, the system moved ashore near Ongole, Andhra Pradesh early on October 28, and then rapidly weakened over land, degenerating into a remnant low the next day.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Heavy rainfall affected coastal Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu, with the storm bringing several days of heavy rainfall to southern India.
Main_Event_Annotation: The IMD’s classification—first as a depression and then an upgrade to a deep depression—indicates the event falls under the tropical cyclone category.
Hazards_Annotation: The report details heavy rainfall leading to inundation in low-lying areas, flooded crop fields, collapsed houses, and widespread disruption, all indicative of flood hazards.

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: The precursor to the storm brought heavy rainfall to southern Thailand, reaching 417 mm (16.4 in) in Ko Samui. The rains killed 11 people in the country and caused ฿400 million (Thai baht, US$10 million) in damage.
The remnants also dropped heavy rainfall in southern India, with a daily peak of 310 mm (12 in) in Tambaram. The rains flooded several villages in Tamil Nadu, killing 11 people.
The rains killed 11 people in the country and caused ฿400 million (Thai baht, US$10 million) in damage.

Time_Annotation: An area of convection formed on November 26 in the eastern Bay of Bengal. On November 27, the JTWC classified the system as Tropical Cyclone 07B, and on the following day the IMD quickly upgraded it to Cyclonic Storm Baaz. It weakened on December 1 and was downgraded to a remnant low on December 2, with remnants later crossing the Indian coast on December 3.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The precursor to the storm brought heavy rainfall to southern Thailand (Ko Samui received 417 mm of rain with 11 fatalities) and the remnants caused heavy rainfall and flooding in southern India (villages in Tamil Nadu were flooded, killing 11 people).
Main_Event_Annotation: The system was initially classified as Tropical Cyclone 07B by the JTWC and was upgraded by the IMD to Cyclonic Storm Baaz, indicating a Tropical Storm/Cyclone event.
Hazards_Annotation: The IMD estimated peak 3-minute winds of 85 km/h, and the heavy rainfall associated with the storm led to flooding in both Thailand and India.

Time_Annotation: Late on June 3, 2009, a cold-core non-tropical low pressure area located over the Baltic Sea collided with a warm air mass, creating atmospheric instability.

Main_Event_Annotation: The text notes that a supercell spawned a tornado in Krasnozavodsk which reached F3 intensity and was the first intense tornado to impact the Moscow region in nearly 25 years.

Forty-two homes were damaged by the tornado, ranging from roof damage to severe interior damage.

Time_Annotation: A strong area of winds near the equator developed an area of convection on November 14 to the east-north-east of Diego Garcia, becoming a tropical depression late on November 14. After turning to the north-east on November 25, Boura dissipated a day later north of Madagascar.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Boura passed just north of St. Brandon on November 19, producing 54.5 mm of rainfall and wind gusts of 106 km/h. It also generated wind gusts of 118 km/h on Mauritius and 111 km/h on Réunion, and later dissipated north of Madagascar.
Main_Event_Annotation: Early on November 15, MFR upgraded the system to Tropical Storm Boura, and later that day the JTWC initiated advisories on Tropical Cyclone 03S; on November 17, Boura intensified into a tropical cyclone.
Hazards_Annotation: The cyclone produced significant wind hazards, with gusts reported at 106 km/h on St. Brandon and 118 km/h and 111 km/h on Mauritius and Réunion, respectively.

Time_Annotation: On 13 May, the Joint Typhoon Warning Center began monitoring a low-level circulation which persisted 588 nm east-northeast of Comoros, stating it was in a favourable environment to intensify. The JTWC also issued their final warning early on May 22 as Ialy was about to fall below tropical storm strength and was starting to rapidly dissipate just offshore Kenya.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: In Kenya, the cyclone killed two people. Strong winds tore off the roof of a school, killing a girl and injuring four others, while another person died due to a fallen wall. Ialy is notable for being the strongest cyclone to have ever affected Kenyan waters and the first to directly affect the country since the beginning of reliable records.
Main_Event_Annotation: Soon afterwards, the MMS received the name Ialy after the agency upgraded the system into a tropical storm. The JTWC then also recognised the system as a cyclone, issuing warnings on it as Tropical Cyclone 24S. Ialy battled through high shear and became a Tropical Cyclone per MFR and a Category 1-equivalent cyclone per JTWC during the afternoon of May 21 local time.
Hazards_Annotation: Strong winds tore off the roof of a school, killing a girl and injuring four others, while another person died due to a fallen wall.

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: Gathering strength, the tornado moved quickly into Newton Falls in Trumbull County causing F3 to F4 damage through much of the town. While nearly 400 homes were heavily damaged or destroyed, no fatalities were recorded in Newton Falls.
Continuing east, the tornado reached F5 intensity as it tore through the north side of Niles. Hundreds of homes in the Niles area were destroyed, including several with anchor bolts swept away.
The Niles Park Plaza shopping center was completely leveled and partially swept away at F5 intensity, with several fatalities occurring at that location.
A nearby retirement home in the Niles area was leveled during the tornado.
A skating rink in the Niles area was also leveled as the tornado passed through.
In Wheatland, Pennsylvania, a steel-frame trucking plant was obliterated and partially swept away at F5 intensity; its steel girder frame was mangled into a pile and pushed off the foundation.

In Kansas, three persons died due to car crashes in icy conditions.[6]
In Kentucky, three people died; two died as a result of car accidents, while the other person was homeless, which caused them to die to exposure.[69]
Missouri had three deaths from vehicular collisions[73][74]
Nebraska had one.[74]
In Wisconsin, one person died from a traffic collision[89]
In Wisconsin, another died from falling through ice on a river.[90]
In northern Frederick County, Maryland, a man died after a tree fell on his car while he was driving west on MD 77.[70]
In Pennsylvania, a person died when trees and hydro poles fell onto their car.[83]
Vermont also had a person die when a tree fell on them.[78]
In Ohio, an accident involving more than 50 vehicles on the eastbound lanes of the Ohio Turnpike in Sandusky County closed the highway for multiple hours and caused four fatalities.[91]
Four people died in other vehicular collisions,[77]
A utility worker was electrocuted while trying to restore power[78]
A 72-year-old woman died from exposure.[79]
A family of six also died in a house fire where they were using unsafe heating methods.[80]
In Colorado, six people, four in Colorado Springs,[67] and two in Denver,[66] reportedly died from exposure to the cold.
In Colorado, six people, four in Colorado Springs,[67] and two in Denver,[66] reportedly died from exposure to the cold.
Georgia had two deaths from exposure,[68]
Tennessee had one death.[87]
Mississippi had one death.[72]
South Dakota had one death.[86]
In South Carolina, one person died when his oxygen machine would not function due to lost power.[84]
In South Carolina, another died from exposure while fixing a pipe to his house.[84]
In mid-Michigan, three people died from cardiac arrest while shoveling or blowing snow.[71]
In mid-Michigan, one person died from carbon monoxide poisoning while in their car.[71]
The intense blizzard in the Buffalo, New York, region caused 34 deaths in Buffalo.[75][76][92]
The intense blizzard in the Buffalo, New York, region caused 7 deaths in Cheektowaga.[75][76][92]
One of the two additional deaths in New York was from carbon monoxide poisoning in Lockport, near Niagara Falls.[75][76]
Another additional death in New York has no specified location.[75][76]
In southwestern Ontario, two people died from exposure.[65]

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: In the Chicago area, the extreme cold and storm conditions caused transit disruptions, including service suspension on the South Shore for the afternoon on December 23, with both the CTA and Metra reporting issues with freezing track switches and mechanical failures.[140]

In the Chicago area, service was suspended on December 24 due to extreme cold and storm conditions affecting transit operations, with CTA and Metra reporting freezing track switches and mechanical failures.[140]

In the Buffalo-Niagara area, all transit service was suspended from the morning of December 23 until the morning of December 27, with reduced Metro Rail Service restarting thereafter and some bus service resuming on December 28.[141][142]

In the New York Metropolitan Area, trains experienced delays due to flooding. The Long Beach Branch of the Long Island Rail Road was shut down between Penn Station and Long Beach, the Metro North Hudson line was temporarily suspended between Poughkeepsie and Peekskill, New Jersey Transit experienced up to 30-minute delays, the Staten Island Ferry was suspended for around an hour, and all buses in Queens were delayed with the Q53-SBS totally suspended.[143][126][144]

In Ontario, GO Transit implemented its snow plan on December 23—reducing peak train service, suspending express trains, and canceling some buses in the Niagara Region—and the Toronto Transit Commission suspended service at 41 bus stops and on Line 3 Scarborough for December 23.[145]
In the Seattle area, a storm led to all buses operated by King County Metro and Sound Transit being canceled due to icy road conditions, and the Seattle Center Monorail was also suspended.[101]
BC Transit suspended all bus service to Victoria for the day.[146]

Time_Annotation: The origin of this major hurricane was traced to a tropical disturbance that moved into the western Caribbean Sea by October 11, 1944. Some re‐intensification occurred as the system traversed the Labrador Sea and Greenland before it merged with the Icelandic Low on October 24.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The cyclone affected Cuba (passing over Isla de la Juventud and making landfall on mainland Cuba), the United States (landfall near Sarasota, passing east of Tampa Bay, and affecting Georgia and South Carolina), Canada (with its remnants passing over Nova Scotia), and Greenland (as it traversed the Labrador Sea and over Greenland).
Main_Event_Annotation: The system developed from a tropical disturbance into a tropical depression, quickly intensified to a tropical storm, and then strengthened into a hurricane, which is characteristic of a Tropical Storm/Cyclone event.
Hazards_Annotation: The report highlights high wind speeds, with sustained winds peaking at 96 mph (154 km/h), gusts up to 118 mph (190 km/h), and a peak intensity wind of 145 mph (233 km/h), identifying Wind as the primary hazard.

Time_Annotation: The final known storm of the season originated from an area of unsettled weather that began affecting ships in the western Caribbean Sea on October 27. Reanalysis could not confirm the existence of a tropical cyclone until October 30, and maritime reports indicate that it achieved minimal hurricane intensity by the following day before moving onshore on November 1. Later, after reaching the southern Gulf of Mexico, the storm turned southwest by November 2 with its track ending east of Cancún two days later.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The storm was centered about 40 mi (65 km) northeast of Honduras's Swan Islands and moved onshore just north of the British Honduras (modern-day Belize)-Mexico border, with its final track ending east of Cancún (Mexico).
Main_Event_Annotation: Chenoweth proposes that this storm began as a tropical storm over the south-central Caribbean on October 27, and the system remains a hurricane despite its passage over the Yucatán Peninsula, indicating it is a tropical cyclone.
Hazards_Annotation: Maritime reports suggest that the storm achieved minimal hurricane intensity, which implies the presence of strong winds – the primary hazard associated with tropical storms/cyclones.

Time_Annotation: The text states: 'The season started on November 1, 1999, and ended for most of the basin on April 30, 2000; for Mauritius and the Seychelles, the season continued until May 15.'
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The article notes that storms struck Mozambique ('...two storms – Leon–Eline and Hudah – struck Mozambique'), made the strongest landfall along eastern Madagascar, Cyclone Connie passed near Réunion, and mentions deaths in Zimbabwe and South Africa. Main_Event_Annotation: The description of the '1999–2000 South-West Indian Ocean tropical cyclone season' along with references to multiple tropical cyclones (Leon–Eline, Hudah, Astride, Babiola, Connie, Gloria, Innocente) indicates a Tropical Storm/Cyclone event.
